title: The big issue behind evidence about learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton argues that any school serious about learning must answer a set of questions about evidence: what counts, who sees it, how it is shared, whether it serves both development and monitoring, and whether gathering it saves time. He sets out six big ideas, using a football coaching team as an analogy for why real-time evidence matters beyond the league table. He insists on consistency of language and approach across a school, on teachers asking whether their students learned rather than how the lesson went, and on students reflecting on their own learning. Leaders should use the same simple questions as teachers when visiting classrooms, and professional development should flow from that classroom evidence. He ends by describing a simple three-by-four chart of knowledge, skills and understanding against new, consolidating, treading water and drowning.
points: Evidence gathered long after teaching, such as tests and exams, must be complemented by evidence of learning in real time, just as a coach watches the match and not only the league table.
Common language and a shared protocol make evidence reliable across a school, especially a large one with many teachers.
The reflective question for teachers should be whether most students learned well, not how the lesson went or how much was covered.
Leaders, teachers and students should use the same questions so that conversations about learning share a thread.
Professional development is strongest when it arises from classroom observation evidence, and a simple three-by-four chart can make this workable.
quotes: Evidence is linked to learning like cheese is linked to onion in the crisp world. They are inseparable.

It’s because it’s only when the players are in action that they can see what is really happening. Our team might have let in more goals than we should have but it is only by watching the team in action that we can see what is happening that causes us to let in goals.

Evidence matters in schools but it can’t only be evidence that is gathered long after the learning has taken place. There has to be evidence of whether learning is happening during real time, when the children, students and teachers are in action.

The most important reflective question for teachers is not: ‘How did that lesson/this morning/last week/last term go?’ It is: ‘Did the majority of my children or students learn well in that lesson or over the past week?’ and, additionally: ‘Were they learning (or not) what I hoped they would learn?

So children and students need help to gather evidence about their own learning and then to reflect on how it went and why. Given the need for consistency (see above) it would be crazy if the way children and students began to think about their own learning was substantially different from that of their teachers.

I have said before that if, as a school leader or manager, I was only allowed one kind of evidence about learning in my school, it would be the answers to those four questions. There is much more I should know and I would know, but if I knew where learning was regularly happening or not and had some idea about why it might or might not be happening, I would sleep much better.

Professional development in schools should be primarily focused around issues that arise directly from observations of whether learning is happening (or not) in real time. It should address those issues in a way that will help improve what is happening in the learning game.
